prompt: A customer asks you to buy their groceries and offers to send you their card PIN and a one-time PIN (OTP) so you can pay. What do you do?

options.text: Accept the PIN and OTP but delete the message afterwards.
Refuse, explain you never accept PINs, OTPs or passwords, and agree a secure payment method instead.
Accept only the OTP, because it expires quickly.
Ask for the card's security code instead, which is safer.

prompt: A friend offers to lend you their catering certificate to upload during verification so you can be approved faster. What is correct?

options.text: Upload it — the certificate is genuine, just not yours.
Upload it and mention it in your bio.
Never submit someone else's or altered documents. Upload only your own evidence or describe your experience honestly.
Edit your name onto a scan of the certificate.

prompt: A customer gave you R1 500 for their weekly shop and you spent R1 230. What happens to the remaining R270?

options.text: Keep it as a tip because the customer did not ask about it.
Use it to start the next customer's shopping, then repay it later.
Record it and return it, or apply it only as the customer specifically instructs.
Spend it on fuel for the trip.

prompt: The outfit the customer approved is sold out in their size. You message them but they haven't replied. What do you do?

options.text: Buy a similar item in a different brand — silence means they trust you.
Pause, keep trying to reach them, and only substitute after their specific recorded approval.
Buy the next size up because it will probably fit.
Buy a more expensive alternative and add the difference to their bill.

prompt: A customer asks you to send money from their bank app on your phone while you are shopping. What do you do?

options.text: Log in with their credentials if they dictate the password carefully.
Refuse. Never handle customer banking logins, PINs or OTPs; use an agreed prepaid or transfer method instead.
Do it once if they watch over video call.
Save their login for next week's shop to save time.

prompt: Someone who is not a PSSA member asks to use a copy of your verified badge on their WhatsApp profile. What is correct?

options.text: Allow it if they pay you a fee.
Allow it only for family.
Refuse. The badge is personal; lending or sharing it is badge misuse.
Allow it if they add a disclaimer.

prompt: A customer pays a deposit for a sourcing job. Before work starts they cancel within the agreed free-cancel window. What should you do with the deposit?

options.text: Keep the full deposit as a lesson.
Follow the written cancellation terms you gave them and refund or retain only what those terms allow.
Keep half automatically, even if your terms say otherwise.
Ignore them until they leave a review.

prompt: You see a social account using a fake PSSA certificate number and claiming to be you. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore it — fake accounts are common.
Report it through PSSA's complaint channels and gather evidence; do not confront with threats.
Post their home address so customers avoid them.
Create a second fake account to confuse them.

prompt: You want to show a beautifully organised wardrobe on your profile, but it is a stock photo, not your work. What is acceptable?

options.text: Use it without comment — customers know photos are illustrative.
Only use it if it is clearly labelled as illustrative, or use photos of your own work with permission.
Edit it slightly so it looks original.
Add fake reviews next to it to build trust.

prompt: Your verification has expired and renewal is not yet approved. What should happen to the verified badge on your social media?

options.text: Keep it until the renewal is approved — it is only a formality.
Stop claiming active verification immediately and remove the badge within two business days.
Replace it with a screenshot of the old certificate.
Change the expiry date on the image.

prompt: A customer raises a complaint about a booking. What are the service targets?

options.text: Acknowledge within two business days and give a substantive response or plan within five business days.
Reply only if they leave a bad review.
Acknowledge within 30 days.
Ask them to withdraw the complaint before you respond.

prompt: A customer leaves a fair, truthful two-star review. Which response is appropriate?

options.text: Offer a refund only if they delete the review.
Post their address so others know who complained.
Respond professionally, address the concern and keep a working channel open.
Block them so they cannot follow up on the order.

prompt: You finish decluttering a customer's home and the result looks amazing. Can you post photos of their home to promote your services?

options.text: Yes, as long as their face isn't visible.
Only with their separate, specific permission for marketing use.
Yes — they booked you, so consent is implied.
Yes, if you blur the street number.

prompt: Before a customer commits to a paid booking, what should they have received?

options.text: A verbal estimate only.
A written summary of the service, complete price breakdown, timing, responsibilities and cancellation terms.
Nothing — details can be agreed after the work is done.
A price that may change without notice.

prompt: You are already booked from 10:00 to 12:00 and receive a request for 11:00 the same day. What do you do?

options.text: Accept both and rush each job.
Accept it and send a friend to the first job without telling the customer.
Decline or suggest another time — only accept work you can reasonably fulfil.
Accept it and cancel the first customer at the last minute.

prompt: Your cousin, who is not verified, offers to take some of your bookings using your profile. Is that allowed?

options.text: Yes, if they are family.
No. Verification cannot be lent; they must register and be verified themselves.
Yes, if you share the earnings.
Yes, but only for small jobs.

prompt: You will arrive 40 minutes late because of a taxi strike. What is the right approach?

options.text: Say nothing and arrive when you can.
Tell the customer promptly, explain honestly and propose a revised time they can accept or decline.
Tell the customer you are already outside.
Mark the booking as completed to avoid a complaint.

prompt: You and the customer agree a refund for a cancelled errand. When should you initiate it?

options.text: Within five business days after the amount is confirmed, using the original payment route where practical.
Only after the customer posts a positive review.
Whenever your next payment comes in.
After charging a release fee.

prompt: Ingredients for a private dinner will cost more than the maximum the customer approved. What do you do?

options.text: Buy them and add the difference to the invoice.
Get the customer's approval before exceeding the agreed maximum.
Use cheaper ingredients without telling them.
Cancel the booking without notice.

prompt: Which statement best reflects how customers must be treated?

options.text: Fairly, respectfully and without unlawful discrimination, using clear language and no pressure tactics.
Regular customers can receive better treatment than new ones on safety matters.
Pressure is acceptable if it closes the booking quickly.
You may refuse customers based on their language or background.

prompt: You spend customer funds on approved items. What should you keep and share?

options.text: Nothing — the finished delivery is enough.
Clear records and receipts (or equivalent proof) for what was spent, shared as agreed with the customer.
Only photos of the shopping bags.
A rough total messaged days later.

prompt: A customer asks you mid-job to also collect a prescription for a relative who is not on the order. What do you do?

options.text: Do it quietly to be helpful.
Confirm whether it is within the agreed scope, get clear approval and update the written summary if needed.
Refuse every change, even written ones.
Charge double without telling them.

prompt: A new customer wants to hand over cash in a deserted parking lot at night. What is the better approach?

options.text: Agree — cash jobs are normal.
Suggest a safer public place or a traceable payment method, and decline arrangements that feel unsafe.
Ask them to come to your home instead.
Bring a friend to intimidate them.

prompt: A customer asks for proof you are verified. What should you point them to?

options.text: A screenshot of an old badge image.
Your live PSSA certificate check (PSSA-YYYY-XXXXXX) so they can confirm current status themselves.
A WhatsApp status that says "verified".
A friend's certificate number.

prompt: A store offers you a personal kickback if you steer the customer to their brand without telling the customer. What do you do?

options.text: Take it — commissions are normal.
Refuse hidden kickbacks; recommend options based on the customer's brief and disclose any relevant arrangement.
Take it and raise the customer's price.
Take it only in cash.

prompt: After a job you still have copies of the customer's ID and bank proof from an earlier chat. What is the right approach?

options.text: Keep them forever for "your records".
Keep personal documents only as long as needed for the purpose, then delete or return them according to privacy rules.
Post them in a private group for backup.
Sell the contact list later.

prompt: The customer asks whether delivery is included. You are unsure. What should you do?

options.text: Say yes and figure it out later.
Check your offer, answer clearly in writing, and update the order summary before they pay.
Ignore the question.
Say no to avoid commitment, even if your listing includes delivery.

prompt: You advertised same-day service but you are fully booked. A customer messages at noon. What do you do?

options.text: Promise same-day anyway and hope.
Be honest about availability and offer the next real slot or decline.
Accept and ghost them if you cannot make it.
Blame traffic later without warning.

prompt: A customer asks you to buy alcohol for a party and you are not sure the recipient is of legal age. What do you do?

options.text: Buy it anyway — it is their responsibility.
Refuse unless you can verify legal age and that the purchase is lawful; do not buy restricted items for underage people.
Ask a stranger outside the shop to buy it.
Buy it and leave it at the gate unsigned.

prompt: Important changes to price, timing or scope are agreed on a quick voice call. What should you do next?

options.text: Rely on memory only.
Confirm the change in writing (message or updated order summary) so both sides have a record.
Change the invoice later without telling them.
Delete the chat history so nothing can be disputed.
